newsitem.title: USA: U.S. obsession with adultery harks back to Puritans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. obsession with adultery harks back to Puritans.

text.p: Despite the obsession with adultery among the U.S. power elite, the embodiment of this sin is not ex-bomber pilot Kelly Flinn or Gen. Joe Ralston or even Bill Clinton. For Americans, it's still Hester Prynne.

Prynne, who slept with a self-righteous minister and bore his child, was forced to wear a red A on her bodice in "The Scarlet Letter," Nathaniel Hawthorne's 19th century novel of 17th century sexual repression and hypocrisy.

The Puritans who ran Massachusetts Bay Colony in those early times made adultery punishable by death, along with such transgressions as witchcraft and fomenting rebellion. That law drew on specific Bible passages for its authority.
These days, the penalty is often more political, as public figures wrestle with an issue perhaps best kept private.
Flinn, the first woman bomber pilot, got a less than honourable discharge from the Air Force after admitting she had an affair with a married civilian and then lied about it to superior officers.
Ralston, once considered all but certain to head the military Joint Chiefs of Staff, found his position under fire after an early extra-marital liaison came to light.

In Georgia, a candidate for governor resigned his commission in the Air National Guard after revealing he had carried on an adulterous relationship for more than a decade. He did not, however, abandon the race for governor.
Clinton managed to win the White House, twice, despite persistent whispers of extra-marital involvement.

One expert on the statistics of adultery said this may be because most Americans believe it should be kept behind closed doors, as long as the adulterer is contrite and the wronged spouse is forgiving.

Americans overwhelmingly disapprove of adultery, with 79 to 80 percent saying such behaviour is always wrong, said Tom Smith of the National Opinion Research Centre at the University of Chicago, which tracks such figures.

This is an increase from the 1970s, when the sexual revolution was at its height and the disapproval rate was 70 to 72 percent, Smith said by telephone. The increase may be due more to the threat of AIDS to the wronged spouse and children than to changing mores, he said.
Between 20 percent and 25 percent of married Americans say they have committed adultery at least once, Smith said.
"(Americans) see it as a sin, a sin that is not systematically violated but not a rarity either," he said, denying that this necessarily makes Americans hypocritical.

"What people are saying is that this is wrong but the temptation is great and it's part of being human that we fall into temptation. The extra thing about adultery is that if a person admits they were wrong and the spouse forgives ... that's their business," Smith said.
As for the Puritans, Peter Drummey, librarian at the Massachusetts Historical Society, said it was not quite accurate to paint them as hostile to passion.

"The Puritans are an extremely complicated group of people and one thing that gets confused is their very stringent moral code, which is perceived as making them anti-sexuality," Drummey said in a telephone interview. "The law in fact set the boundaries."

Whatever its history, Smith acknowledged that adultery among public figures is a bigger deal in the United States than elsewhere, notably France, England and Latin America, where he said extramarital affairs are often tolerated.
